Ms. Jackson: The next thing I would like to talk about is how Mother came to America.
Mr. Taylor: Excuse me, Ms. Jackson. If you would be so kind, I'm going to have to ask you to stop now.
Ms. Jackson: If you will wait for a moment, Mr. Taylor, I'll be finished shortly.
Mr. Taylor: I'm sorry, Ms. Jackson. I reckon this is the third time I've had to interrupt you. I wondered whether you heard me the first two times. I believe that here at Toastmaster's, we have a very strict time limit for each speech: only 10 minutes. Your speech is going on 20 minutes now.
Ms. Jackson: Well, I don't know whether I should follow such a silly rule. I just can't leave the audience hanging.

Mr. Taylor: I believe that if anyone is that interested, they can ask you at the next break. Now, if you will please leave the stage, Ms. Jackson, we can continue with another speaker.
Ms. Jackson: What can a person be expected to say in such a short time?
Mr. Taylor: For goodness' sakes. Those are the rules, Ms. Jackson.
Ms. Jackson: For heaven's sake! Why do I have to stop?

Mr. Taylor: Because I said so, and I'm the master of ceremonies! If you won't leave now I will ask for a security guard!
Ms. Jackson: Well, if you will raise your voice like that, I'm never coming back again.
Mr. Taylor: My goodness. Next I would like to introduce Ms. Janet Kerry who will talk about how to make beeswax.
Ms. Kerry: Umm ... I'm afraid I'm a bit embarrassed, but to tell you the truth, I can't find my speaking notes. I can't remember whether I left them at home or at work, and now I'm so flustered I just don't know what to say.
Ms. Jackson: I can continue! So, as I was saying, my mother, such a brave woman, came to America ...

You can use whether or if to talk about situations where two alternatives are possible. There are some instances, however, where it is more common to use whether only.
Whether is similar to if so you can use either when two options are discussed or thought about. You can also use whether or if when people are not certain about something.

Maria didn't know if/whether she should invite Salvador to the wedding. He was her ex-boyfriend and he didn't like her fiancé. She was trying to decide if/whether inviting him would be the best decision.
We can use verbs like discuss, choose, consider, determine, think about, wonder, know, and debate when we want to talk about two or more alternatives.
You use whether before an infinitive (to + verb), not if.
Maria considered whether to invite her ex-boyfriend to the wedding.
Some verbs that are not used with whether and the infinitive are: ask, explain, realize, conclude, speculate, imagine and think.
There is also a difference between whether and that.

I didn't know whether he had gotten the email. (if he had gotten the email or not)
I didn't know that he had gotten the email. (he had gotten the email)
I wondered whether you heard me the first two times.
Well, I don't know whether I should follow such a silly rule.
You can use the first conditional with special modal verbs to express refusal and polite requests.

You use the first conditional to talk about possibility of things in the present and future.
Do you remember how to form this conditional?
Do you remember when to use commas?

Look at the sentences below and try to answer the above questions.
  • If Emilio passes his exam, he will have a party.
  • I will go to the beach if the weather is nice.

You can use modals instead of will in the first conditional as well. This changes the meaning slightly.
  • If Emilio passes his exam, he should have a party. (more of a suggestion)
  • I may/might go to the beach if the weather is nice. (less certainty than will)

You can also insert modals into the if-clause.
  • If you will hold on for just a second, I'll go get Miguel. (polite request)
  • If you will hold my suitcase, I'll find my passport. (polite request)
  • If you will lend me $50, I won't have to go to the bank. (willingness to do something)
  • If you won't play Monopoly with me, I'll ask someone else to play. (refusal to do something)
  • If you will raise your voice like that, I'm never coming back again. (strong disapproval)
 Stress the won't in speaking for the refusal.
If you will be so kind, I'm going to have to ask you to stop now.
If you will wait for a moment, Mr. Taylor, I'll be finished shortly.
to not finish telling a story
Example:  I just can't leave the audience hanging.
These are words you use when you have to interrupt a person giving a speech.
to be close to reaching a certain length of time
Example: Your speech is going on 20 minutes now.
a person who speaks at a public event
Example: Ms Jackson, we can continue with another speaker.
Example: For goodness' sakes. Those are the rules, Ms. Jackson.
Example: For heaven's sake! Why do I have to stop?
use your voice in an aggressive way, such as to yell
Example: Well, if you will raise your voice like that, I'm never coming back again.
One person is the official master of ceremonies of a Toastmaster's Club meeting. The other person is giving a speech. It is taking too long.
Use the modal 'will' to make a polite request (at first) and then to show strong disapproval.
Use expressions to show annoyance, like 'For heaven's sake' or 'For Pete's sake'.
